label: The Principal Curvatures of a Surface
notes: This chapter, printed pages 109 through 114, asks how every direction of bending at one surface point can be organized. We slice the surface with vertical planes, read off a curvature for each slice, and discover that two orthogonal directions carry the extreme values from which all others follow.

label: Normal Sections
notes: Pick a point and erect the surface normal there. Any plane containing that normal cuts the surface in a plane curve called a normal section. The signed curvature of that curve at the point is the normal curvature for its direction, and it changes smoothly as the cutting plane rotates.

label: Sign of Normal Curvature
notes: We orient normal curvature against the chosen unit normal. A section bending toward the normal counts as positive, one bending away as negative. On a saddle some directions curve up while others curve down, so the normal curvature must change sign as the cutting plane sweeps around the point.

label: The Normal-Section Fan
notes: Sweeping the cutting plane through every direction produces a fan of normal sections sharing one tangent point. Reading their curvatures in order reveals a single smooth maximum and a single smooth minimum, hinting that the bending data is governed by a simple two-number law rather than infinitely many independent slopes.

label: Principal Curvatures
notes: The largest and smallest normal curvatures at a point are the principal curvatures kappa one and kappa two. The directions in which these extremes occur are the principal directions. Euler proved these two privileged directions are always orthogonal, so they frame the tangent plane with a natural perpendicular coordinate cross.

label: Euler's Formula
notes: Euler's formula gives the normal curvature of an oblique section as kappa one cosine squared theta plus kappa two sine squared theta, where theta is measured from the first principal direction. Every directional curvature is thus a weighted blend of just the two extremes, with the weights summing to one.

label: Why the Formula Holds
notes: In principal coordinates the second fundamental form is diagonal, so the height of the surface above its tangent plane is a pure sum of squared coordinates with coefficients kappa one and kappa two. Plugging a unit tangent at angle theta into this quadratic and doubling recovers Euler's cosine-sine expression directly.

label: The Curvature Rose
notes: Plotting normal curvature against direction traces a smooth closed rose. Its two perpendicular axes of symmetry are exactly the principal directions, and its longest and shortest radii read off kappa one and kappa two. The whole continuum of bending is compressed into this single two-lobed picture.

label: Mean and Gaussian Curvature
notes: From the two principals we build two famous combinations. Their average is the mean curvature H, sensitive to how the surface sits in space, while their product is the Gaussian curvature K. Gauss later proved K is intrinsic, surviving any bending that does not stretch the surface fabric.

label: Sign of K and Local Shape
notes: The sign of the Gaussian product classifies the point. Both principals agreeing gives positive K and a dome or bowl; opposite signs give negative K and a saddle; one principal vanishing gives zero K and a cylinder-like ridge that bends only one way while staying flat along the other.

label: Surface of Revolution Lab
notes: On a surface of revolution the principal directions align with meridians and parallels by symmetry. The meridian supplies one principal curvature directly, while the circular parallel supplies the other through its normal section. Computing both lets us read mean and Gaussian curvature at every height along the profile.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: We reduced infinitely many normal sections to two principal curvatures and Euler's blending law. The orthogonal principal directions frame the tangent plane, while H and K package the pair into shape and intrinsic invariants. Next we follow Gauss in proving K depends only on the surface metric.
